note: Mark's chief priests resolve {mk 14:2 Μὴ ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ} (“not during the festival”), yet the arrest happens during the festival anyway, an irony Mark leaves unspoken. John gives the plot a political motive: {jn 11:48 ἐλεύσονται οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι καὶ ἀροῦσιν ἡμῶν καὶ τὸν τόπον καὶ τὸ ἔθνος} (“the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation”). Caiaphas then says more than he knows: {jn 11:50 ἵνα εἷς ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ} (“that one man should die for the people”).

A rare, striking verbal link between Mark and John: both describe the ointment with the same unusual phrase, {mk 14:3 μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς} (“ointment of *pistic* nard”) and {jn 12:3 μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς}. *Pistikēs* appears nowhere else in Greek of the time; it may mean “genuine” or derive from the pistachio. Both also price it at {mk 14:5 δηναρίων τριακοσίων} (“three hundred denarii”). Mark's woman is anonymous, though Jesus promises {mk 14:9 εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς} (“in memory of her”). John names her Mary.

Mark has one animal, a {mk 11:2 πῶλον} (“colt”). Matthew has two, {mt 21:2 ὄνον δεδεμένην καὶ πῶλον μετ αὐτῆς} (“a donkey and a colt with her”), because he reads Zechariah 9:9's poetic parallelism literally: {mt 21:5 ἐπὶ ὄνον καὶ ἐπὶ πῶλον} (“on a donkey **and** on a colt”). Only John mentions {jn 12:13 τὰ βαΐα τῶν φοινίκων} (“palm branches”). Luke drops the Hebrew “Hosanna” and echoes the angels at the nativity: {lk 19:38 ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰρήνη καὶ δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις} (“peace in heaven and glory in the highest”).

Only Luke has Jesus weep over the city as he approaches: {lk 19:42 Εἰ ἔγνως ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ καὶ σὺ τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην} (“if only you had known on this day the things that make for peace”). It is a pun, since Jerusalem was popularly etymologized as “city of peace”. The oracle describes a siege, embankment and all, and ends {lk 19:44 οὐκ ἔγνως τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς σου} (“you did not recognize the time of your **visitation**”), echoing 1:68 and 7:16.

Mark adds a puzzling remark: Jesus found nothing but leaves, {mk 11:13 ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς οὐκ ἦν σύκων} (“for it was not the season for figs”). Why curse a tree for being out of season? The answer seems to be symbolic: Mark wraps the temple scene between the cursing and the withering, so the tree stands for the temple. Matthew drops the awkward remark and has the tree wither {mt 21:19 παραχρῆμα} (“at once”), dissolving Mark's sandwich.

The Synoptics place this at the end of Jesus' ministry, as the trigger for his arrest; John places it at the beginning (chapter 2). Mark quotes Isaiah 56:7 in full: {mk 11:17 οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται πᾶσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν} (“a house of prayer **for all the nations**”). Matthew and Luke both drop “for all the nations”. John's Jesus objects to {jn 2:16 οἶκον ἐμπορίου} (“a house of trade”) and says {jn 2:19 Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον} (“destroy this temple”), a saying the Synoptics place in the mouths of false witnesses.

Peter notices the next morning: {mk 11:21 ἡ συκῆ ἣν κατηράσω ἐξήρανται} (“the fig tree you cursed has withered”). The lesson that follows is about faith that can say {mk 11:23 τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ Ἄρθητι} (“to **this** mountain, be lifted up”), perhaps the Temple Mount itself. Mark adds a saying on forgiveness that echoes the Lord's Prayer, which his Gospel otherwise lacks: {mk 11:25 ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς} (“your Father in heaven”). Later manuscripts add verse 26.

Among the most closely copied debates in the triple tradition: around 70% of Matthew's words are Mark's. Jesus answers with a counter-question: {mk 11:30 τὸ βάπτισμα τὸ Ἰωάννου ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἦν ἢ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων} (“John's baptism: from heaven or from humans?”). “Heaven” is a reverent substitute for “God”. Five small minor agreements, such as both Matthew and Luke adding that Jesus was **teaching** in the temple, show the later evangelists editing together.

Only Matthew has this parable: one son says no but goes to work, the other says yes but doesn't go. The verdict: {mt 21:31 οἱ τελῶναι καὶ αἱ πόρναι προάγουσιν ὑμᾶς} (“tax collectors and prostitutes are going ahead of you into the kingdom”). Manuscripts are notoriously tangled here. Some reverse the order of the sons and correspondingly the answer, and a few even have the leaders give the **wrong** answer. Textual critics still argue over which is original.

An allegory in which nearly everyone recognizes the characters. The owner finally sends {mk 12:6 ἕνα εἶχεν υἱὸν ἀγαπητόν} (“one beloved son”), the words of the baptismal voice. Matthew draws the starkest conclusion: the kingdom {mt 21:43 δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς} (“will be given to a people producing its fruits”). The quotation of Psalm 118, {mk 12:10 Λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες} (“the stone the builders rejected”), may rest on a Hebrew pun: *ben* (son), *eben* (stone).

The questioners open with flattery, {mk 12:14 οὐ γὰρ βλέπεις εἰς πρόσωπον ἀνθρώπων} (literally “you don't look at people's faces”, that is, you show no partiality). Jesus asks to see a coin: {mk 12:16 Τίνος ἡ εἰκὼν αὕτη καὶ ἡ ἐπιγραφή} (“whose **image** is this, and inscription?”). A denarius of Tiberius proclaimed him son of the divine Augustus. Readers who knew Genesis 1:27, where humans bear God's *eikōn*, could hear the second half of the answer as a claim on the whole person.

The Sadducees, who denied resurrection (Josephus and Acts 23:8 agree), pose a riddle about one woman with seven husbands. Mark's Jesus answers bluntly, {mk 12:27 πολὺ πλανᾶσθε} (“you are badly mistaken”). Luke softens that and adds two lines of his own: the risen are {lk 20:36 ἰσάγγελοι} (“like angels”, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament) and {lk 20:38 πάντες γὰρ αὐτῷ ζῶσιν} (“for all live to him”).

Jesus takes the offensive with a riddle from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted or alluded to in the New Testament: {mk 12:36 Εἶπεν κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου} (“the Lord said to my lord”). If David calls the Messiah “lord”, how can he be merely David's son? All three keep this short exchange close to Mark's wording; Matthew and Luke share long runs of identical words with him here.

Mark explains the widow's two coins with a Roman one: {mk 12:42 λεπτὰ δύο ὅ ἐστιν κοδράντης} (“two *lepta*, which make a *quadrans*”). Explaining Greek money in Roman terms is one of the clues that point to an audience in the Roman west, possibly Rome itself. Luke drops the explanation and uses the rare word {lk 21:2 πενιχρὰν} (“needy”). The punchline: she gave {mk 12:44 ὅλον τὸν βίον αὐτῆς} (“her whole **life**”), that is, her whole livelihood.

The discourse begins with a prophecy: {mk 13:2 οὐ μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον} (“not one stone will be left on another”). The Romans destroyed the temple in 70 CE. In Mark and Luke the disciples ask when and what sign. Matthew adds a second question about {mt 24:3 τῆς σῆς παρουσίας} (“your **coming**”). *Parousia*, the technical term for the second coming, appears in the Gospels only in this chapter of Matthew. Mark calls the wars and earthquakes {mk 13:8 ἀρχὴ ὠδίνων} (“the beginning of **birth pains**”).

Mark's {mk 13:10 εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη πρῶτον δεῖ κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον} (“the gospel must **first** be preached to all nations”) becomes in Matthew a timetable: {mt 24:14 καὶ τότε ἥξει τὸ τέλος} (“and **then** the end will come”). Matthew had already used Mark's persecution sayings in his mission speech (10:17–22). Luke's version contains a tension he doesn't resolve: some will be killed, yet {lk 21:18 θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὑμῶν οὐ μὴ ἀπόληται} (“not a hair of your head will perish”).

Mark's {mk 13:14 τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ἑστηκότα} (“the abomination of desolation standing”) uses a **masculine** participle with a neuter noun, as if it were a person. Then he addresses his audience directly: {mk 13:14 ὁ ἀναγινώσκων νοείτω} (“let the **reader** understand”), a sign that this is a written text. Luke replaces the cryptic phrase with plain history: {lk 21:20 κυκλουμένην ὑπὸ στρατοπέδων Ἰερουσαλήμ} (“Jerusalem surrounded by armies”). Only Matthew adds a prayer that flight not come {mt 24:20 μηδὲ σαββάτῳ} (“on a sabbath”).

Matthew merges Mark's warning about false messiahs with Q sayings that Luke places in chapter 17, which accounts for the 57 minor agreements. Matthew's lightning illustrates the {mt 24:27 ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου} (“coming of the Son of Man”). The images of who is “taken” differ: Matthew's {mt 24:40 δύο ἔσονται ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ} (“two in a field”), Luke's {lk 17:34 δύο ἐπὶ κλίνης μιᾶς} (“two in one bed”). Next to the flood comparison, being taken may mean judgment, not rescue.

The climax quotes Daniel 7:13: {mk 13:26 ὄψονται τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενον ἐν νεφέλαις} (“they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds”). Matthew adds {mt 24:30 τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου} (“the **sign** of the Son of Man”), the nations' mourning from Zechariah 12, and {mt 24:31 μετὰ σάλπιγγος μεγάλης} (“with a great trumpet”). Luke adds cosmic anxiety on earth among the nations, {lk 21:25 ἐν ἀπορίᾳ ἤχους θαλάσσης} (“perplexed at the roaring of the sea”).

Matthew and Mark agree in about 89% of their words here, one of the highest scores on the site. The passage holds two of the most debated verses in the Gospels: {mk 13:30 οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη} (“this generation will not pass away”) until all this happens, and {mk 13:32 οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός} (“not even the Son”) knows the day or hour. Luke keeps the first but omits the second entirely; some Matthew manuscripts drop “nor the Son” (see Variants).

A two-verse summary found only in Luke: Jesus taught in the temple by day and spent the nights {lk 21:37 εἰς τὸ ὄρος τὸ καλούμενον Ἐλαιῶν} (“on the mount called Olivet”), and all the people {lk 21:38 ὤρθριζεν} (“came early in the morning”) to hear him. A group of medieval manuscripts (family 13) inserts the story of the woman caught in adultery **right here**, after Luke 21:38, a sign of how that story floated before it settled in John 8.

Only Matthew tells this parable of bridesmaids waiting with lamps: {mt 25:2 πέντε δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἦσαν μωραὶ καὶ πέντε φρόνιμοι} (“five were foolish and five wise”). *Mōrai* gives English “moron”; the same pair of words ended the Sermon on the Mount (the wise and foolish builders). The delay of the bridegroom reflects the early church's experience of the delayed return of Christ. The moral: {mt 25:13 γρηγορεῖτε οὖν} (“so keep awake”).

Only Matthew has this scene, the climax of Jesus' teaching in his Gospel. The Son of Man separates the nations {mt 25:32 ὥσπερ ὁ ποιμὴν ἀφορίζει τὰ πρόβατα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐρίφων} (“as a shepherd separates sheep from goats”). The criterion is care for {mt 25:40 ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων} (“one of the least of these my brothers”). Whether that means anyone in need or specifically Jesus' disciples (as “little ones” and “brothers” often do in Matthew) is a long-running debate.
